profile.reading:
This facility is mapped as Level 3 Communications, retaining the pre-Lumen brand name, at 5400 South Miami Boulevard, Durham, NC 27703, in the Research Triangle Park area; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Level 3 Communications was acquired by CenturyLink on November 1, 2017 and the combined company was renamed Lumen Technologies on September 14, 2020; some legacy facility signage and mapping records, including this one, still carry the pre-merger Level 3 name. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

Durham has moved faster than most North Carolina cities to rein in data center growth: the Durham City Council passed a 60-day moratorium on new data center development on May 4, 2026, citing energy costs, water usage, air quality, and climate impacts, with one councilmember saying he would push for a full 24-month moratorium once state law allows it. Governor Josh Stein separately proposed, on June 15, 2026, phasing out North Carolina's data center sales- and electricity-tax exemptions by 2032, ending the electricity exemption specifically and setting a 2026 application deadline; the state's existing exemptions cost an estimated $45 to $57 million a year currently, a figure Stein's office projected could reach roughly $450 million a year in lost revenue if all proposed North Carolina data centers are built.

Durham sits within North Carolina's Research Triangle, a metro that has drawn both hyperscale campuses and smaller network-edge colocation buildings like this one; the Triangle's university and research-park economy has made local officials especially attentive to weighing data center jobs and tax revenue against energy and water demand, a tension visible in Durham's own May 2026 moratorium vote.

reading.body:
Lumen operates this Durham facility as part of a 175-plus-site North American colocation portfolio under the legacy Level 3 Communications name. Lumen publishes no per-building capacity figures for any of its sites, so this facility's power draw and rack count are unknown. The operator's standard offering across its portfolio is cabinet power ranging from 3 to 15 kilowatts per cabinet, a density typical of network-edge and carrier-neutral colocation rather than hyperscale AI training.

Durham has become hostile to data center expansion. The city council imposed a 60-day moratorium on new data center development in May 2026 citing energy costs, water usage, air quality, and climate impacts, with officials considering a full 24-month moratorium. Governor Josh Stein proposed in June 2026 phasing out North Carolina's data center tax exemptions by 2032, ending the electricity exemption specifically. The state's existing exemptions cost $45 to $57 million annually and could reach $450 million yearly if all proposed facilities are built.

This facility is one of 19 mapped data center sites in North Carolina but ranks outside the five sites with published power capacity. The Research Triangle's economy and regulatory environment have made local officials attentive to the tradeoff between data center employment and tax revenue against energy and water demand. Without published capacity figures, this facility cannot be ranked against the state's 50 megawatts of published capacity or assessed for AI scaling relevance.
